summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that divide.

The counterweight is lethal violence against women and the state's classification of it. The Baja California Attorney General's Office publicly identified Brayan Rivera as a serial perpetrator of feminicides; he was arrested in Downey, California in June 2023 and presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson for provisional extradition detention, with probable cause determined on 29 June 2023. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the attorney general linked him to at least three killings in Tijuana: Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed 24 January 2022 in room 404 of the Hotel Cascadas in the city's tolerance zone, Elizabeth on 14 February, and Karen, 28, on 30 August 2021 at the Motel Hacienda Soler; extradition was then estimated at between 15 days and two years.

Under-counting is the pattern rather than the exception. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in the state while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. Female economic participation in Baja California stands at roughly 46 to 47 per cent, ranking 14th of 32 states.

Mixed assessment: formal recognition law that now reaches adults, minors and non-binary people, alongside a border-city pattern of lethal violence against women that official statistics under-record.
tangentialFactors:
Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" on 18 July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with sentences of up to 70 years; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that nationally over 95 per cent of homicides went unpunished in 2022, and that Mexico is one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people. No equivalent transfemicide offence exists in Baja California's penal code.

Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024, "I Just Want to Contribute to Society", documents how a state that has not reformed behaves: Tabasco has no recognition procedure, lacks hate-motivation provisions in its criminal code, its health staff routinely out patients by using legal names, and the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez remained unsolved. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 in the year to September 2023, second only to Brazil.

Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and cautions that formal rights should not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationally since 2009.
localsOnly:
The recognition procedure is a resident instrument: applicants file under the Civil Code provisions as reformed in 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the 2024 amendment opened the route to people under 18 and to non-binary applicants, so resident documents can now be aligned for minors with parental or guardian involvement.

Residents also live with the under-classification of femicide: of 1,179 women killed in the state during the term of Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila, 110 cases were typified as feminicide, and the state's near-decade backlog of open homicide files was being re-reviewed as of July 2023.

Economic standing is a domestic indicator: female economic participation in Baja California is about 46 to 47 per cent, 14th among the 32 states.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources: whether the Brayan Rivera extradition was completed and the three linked cases concluded; the reporting stops at the July 2023 extradition hearing, and no outcome is sourced.

Not sourced: any Baja California statute specifically criminalising transfemicide, any data on the number of recognition applications granted under the 2022, 2023 or 2024 reforms, and any state-level recording of killings of trans people in Baja California. Transfemicide counts available to this dossier are national or from other states.

Enforcement of the recognition procedure has not been independently assessed in the inventory; Human Rights Watch's March 2025 tracker records the existence of the procedure and the Supreme Court ruling, not implementation quality in this state.
